idiom_name: struct with a separate protected map + AES-GCM sealed blob (crypto/cipher) + MarshalJSON/String hooks
implementation_notes: Go's standard library supplies the parts but not the pattern: crypto/aes plus cipher.NewGCM (or cipher.NewGCMWithRandomNonce, the form the runtime itself now uses) produce the sealed blob, encoding/gob or encoding/json carries it, and the transfer object is a struct whose protected pairs are partitioned and dropped after Seal. What replaces the classic structure: the unexported map plus a custom MarshalJSON/GobEncode pair replaces the class's protected map, and a String() method (fmt.Stringer) is the masking hook for log output, because fmt prints unexported fields by reflection when no Stringer exists. encoding/json marshals only exported fields, so the sealed blob must be an exported field or carry its own marshaler, and the protected map needs an explicit serialization path rather than visibility rules.
pitfalls: encoding/json silently omits unexported fields, so an unexported protected map disappears from the payload (safe) but an unexported sealed blob does too (the field never crosses the boundary) - give the type MarshalJSON/GobEncode instead of relying on visibility.
fmt prints unexported fields through reflection when the type has no String()/Format method, so a log line can expose the plaintext map; implement fmt.Stringer and never log the map directly.

GCM nonces must be unique per key: store the nonce with the ciphertext (the runtime's NewGCMWithRandomNonce exists to make misuse harder), and remember that a nil or ignored error from rand.Read drops straight to a predictable nonce.
Slices are reference values and []byte key/ciphertext copies cannot be wiped in general (string(key) even allocates an immutable copy); zero what you can and treat key lifetime as best-effort.
